y-m-73-01.title: If it rose 50% and then fell 50%
y-m-73-01.topic: Applying percent changes one after another
y-m-73-01.goal: Using the fact that each percent change is based on the value just before it, find the error in a solution that simply added the percents, and build your own combinations of increase and decrease that return to the starting value.
y-m-73-01.material: The daily number of visitors to an online shop rose 50% from the starting number in January, and then fell 50% from the January number in February. Every percent change is based on the number of visitors in the 'month just before'. Take the starting number of visitors to be 100, and treat the results as theoretical values in which decimals are allowed. Below is one student's solution.
y-m-73-01.thinking.0: Finding the contradictory line in the solution
y-m-73-01.thinking.1: Knowing that when the base changes, the same percent becomes a different amount
y-m-73-01.thinking.2: Making several combinations that satisfy the condition
y-m-73-01.prereq.0: Calculating percent increases and decreases by multiplication (middle-school level)
y-m-73-01.prereq.1: Solving by trying out an integer equation
y-m-73-01.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in this solution that is wrong. (Look for the line that gives numbers that do not match.)
y-m-73-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write down how many visitors it says there are, and find two lines that give different numbers for the same month.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check in line 2 and line 3 what number each of +50% and −50% is 50% of.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.line.0: Take the starting number of visitors to be 100.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.line.3: Since +50% and −50% add up to 0%, the number of visitors in February is 100, the same as at the start.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the number of visitors did not change over the two months.
y-m-73-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 already gives 75 visitors for February, but line 4 says 100, so they do not match. The +50% and −50% in line 4 have different bases (the first is based on 100, the second on 150). Percents can be added and subtracted only when they have the same base. So line 4 is wrong, and line 5, which is built on it, is wrong too.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.prompt: Build combinations that return exactly to the starting value. Enter 2 different pairs (p, q) such that the value rises p% in the first month and then falls q% (based on the value at that time) the next month, so that after two months it is exactly the same as at the start. p is an integer from 1 to 500, and q is an integer from 1 to 99.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a p, find the value after the first month, and then try out for yourself what percent you must cut from it to get back to 100.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try whether p and q can be the same, and if not, compare whether q is greater or less than p.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers within the range.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be an integer from 1 to 500, and q must be an integer from 1 to 99.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The value after two months is the same as at the start.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The value after two months is different from the start. First find the value after the first month, and then check the value you get by cutting q% from it.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.explain: Examples: If it rises 25% it becomes 125, and since 20% of 125 is 25, cutting 20% gives 100. If it rises 100% it becomes 200, and cutting 50% gives 100; if it rises 150% it becomes 250, and cutting 60% gives 100. (300, 75) and (400, 80) work too. Because the value after the increase is larger, the percent cut needed to get back is always smaller than the percent increase.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Using one number, explain why p and q are not equal in the combinations you made.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Choose one of the combinations you made above, and first write the value after the first month.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find what q% of that value is, and compare it with q% of the starting value.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The base of the percent cut from 125 is ...
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use in your explanation the fact that the value after the first month differs from the starting value?
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say clearly what the base of the percent cut is?
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate the numbers you used yourself and check that they are right?
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.model.0: The value after the increase becomes greater than 100, so the base of the percent cut changes. If you cut 25% of the value 125 that came from a 25% increase, you get 93.75, so it does not return; you must cut 20%, which is 25, to get 100.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.model.1: In the first month the base is 100, and in the second month the base is the larger value 150. Even for the same 50%, the amount cut is larger at 75, so the percent cut needed to return can be smaller, as the example (150%, 60%) shows.
y-m-73-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Another description with the examples changed

y-m-73-02.title: Is the place with the lowest cost per item the place with the greatest profit?
y-m-73-02.topic: Average cost and the output with the greatest profit
y-m-73-02.goal: Check that the output with the lowest average cost per item and the output with the greatest profit can be different, adjusting your judgment as each piece of price information is given.
y-m-73-02.material:
A handmade soap workshop makes q items (an integer) a month and sells them all. The total cost for one month is C(q) = 50 + 10q + q² (unit: 천 원). Of this, 50 is a fixed cost, which is paid every month even if not a single item is made. Profit = selling price × q − C(q). The average cost per item is C(q) ÷ q. (q² is read as 'q squared'.)

Output q (items) | Total cost (천 원) | Average cost per item (천 원)
1 | 61 | 61.00
3 | 89 | 29.67
5 | 125 | 25.00
7 | 169 | 24.14
8 | 194 | 24.25
10 | 250 | 25.00
15 | 425 | 28.33
20 | 650 | 32.50

(Read the table in the order q, total cost, average cost. Among integer values of q, the lowest average cost is at q=7.)
y-m-73-02.thinking.0: Holding off on a judgment when information is lacking
y-m-73-02.thinking.1: Correcting a judgment with new information
y-m-73-02.thinking.2: Making several values that satisfy the condition
y-m-73-02.prereq.0: Substituting numbers into a quadratic expression
y-m-73-02.prereq.2: Telling apart an average (per-item) value and a total value
y-m-73-02.prereq.3: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.prompt: Price information will be revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose the most fitting judgment for now.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first write down which numbers you know now and which numbers you do not know yet.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.hint.1: Pick two or three numbers and compare them directly to check whether the judgment you chose matches the profit numbers that have been revealed.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.info: You know only the table above. You do not yet know the selling price per item.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we say that 'profit is greatest when making 7 items, where the average cost is lowest'?
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Profit depends on the selling price, so the cost table alone cannot tell you which output gives the larger profit. For now, 'holding off on a judgment' is the best-supported answer.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Yes. At 7 items, where the cost per item is lowest, the profit is also greatest.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You linked low cost directly to high profit. Profit also depends on the selling price, so it cannot be confirmed from the cost table alone.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Without knowing the selling price you cannot calculate profit, so it is too early to judge now.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not forget that profit is the difference between revenue and cost. You pointed out what more information needs to be known.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The fewer items you make below 7, the lower the cost per item, so the greater the profit.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: In the table, the lower outputs (5 items, 3 items) actually have a higher cost per item. You need to check again which way to read the table.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.info: The selling price per item has become known to be 40 (천 원). Calculating profit = 40q − C(q), the profit is 111 if q=7, 150 if q=10, 175 if q=15, 150 if q=20, and 75 if q=25.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How would you judge now? (Within the outputs shown in the table)
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.after: If the selling price is far above the average cost of 24.14, then when you make more than 7 items, the revenue that is added is greater than the cost that is added, so profit increases further. Profit is greatest at 15 items with 175 (counting integers), and then it decreases.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Profit is greatest when making 7 items, where the average cost is lowest.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Larger values than the 111 for 7 items appear at 10 items (150) and 15 items (175). Compare with the numbers you just checked.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The more items you make, the more the profit keeps increasing.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Looking at 20 items (150) and 25 items (75), from some point on the profit decreases. This judgment did not read the table to the end.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Making more than 7 items gives a larger profit, and 15 items is the greatest.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You compared the profit numbers directly and read that the lowest average cost and the greatest profit can be different.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Competition has grown fiercer and the selling price per item has dropped to 24 (천 원). The fixed cost of 50 is still paid this month even if production stops. Profit = 24q − C(q): −50 if q=0, −5 if q=5, −2 if q=6, −1 if q=7, −2 if q=8, and −10 if q=10.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: At this price, what is the most fitting judgment for this month's production plan?
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.after: At a price of 24, every output is a loss. But the fixed cost of 50 is paid anyway, so −1 at 7 items is much better than −50 at 0 items. (If the fixed cost could be avoided, the judgment would change, but in this problem we assumed it cannot be avoided.)
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is a loss, but the loss is smallest at 7 items, so it is better to make them.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You included in the comparison the condition that the fixed cost is paid whether or not you make anything. This differs from a judgment that leaves the fixed cost out.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Every output is a loss, so it is better not to make a single item.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This judgment left out the −50 for not making anything. Under the condition that the fixed cost is paid anyway, also compare the profit at 0 items.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If you make 7 items, where the average cost is lowest, this month will be profitable.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You missed that the average cost of 24.14 is greater than the selling price of 24. Even the lowest average cost is higher than the price.
y-m-73-02.s.s1.reflect: Look back at your three judgments. When was the output with the lowest average cost the same as the output with the greatest profit? When the selling price changed, how did the output with the greatest profit change?
y-m-73-02.s.s2.prompt: When the selling price is 40 (천 원), enter 3 different outputs q whose profit is greater than making 7 items, where the average cost is lowest. (q is an integer from 1 to 30)
y-m-73-02.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a few values of q such as 7, 10, 20, 25, calculate the profit, compare it with 111, and organize it in a table.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.hint.1: To find where it starts to exceed 111 and where it falls below again, change q one at a time and test the boundaries.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.fail.c1: q must be an integer from 1 to 30.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The profit is greater than the 111 at 7 items.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The profit is not greater than 111. Calculate 40q − C(q) and compare it with the 111 at 7 items.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.explain: The profit is −q² + 30q − 50, so it is greater than 111 for q=8 to 22. For example: q=8 gives 126, 10 gives 150, 15 gives 175, and 22 gives 126. q=23 gives 111, which is equal, and 25 gives 75, which is less than at 7 items. The greatest profit is at 15 items (175).
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Using numbers, explain why, when the selling price is 40, the 7 items with the lowest average cost are not the output with the greatest profit.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put 7 items and 10 items side by side in the profit table and look at where the difference between the two profits comes from.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Calculate separately the cost that is added and the revenue that is added when you go from 7 items to 8, and compare them.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: When you make one more item beyond 7 ...
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your explanation that 'average cost per item' and 'profit' are different quantities?
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check the numbers you used in the profit table?
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the fact that the conclusion may change if the selling price changes?
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Average cost is only the cost per item. If the selling price is 40, the extra cost from the 8th item beyond 7 (about 25) is less than 40, so the more you make, the more profit grows. In fact, 7 items give 111 and 15 items give 175.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The price is 40, which is very different from the average cost of 24.14. As long as the extra cost of increasing the number of items is less than the price of 40, making more gives a greater profit. 10 items give 150, which is greater than the 111 for 7 items.
y-m-73-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Another description that puts the extra cost into words

y-m-73-03.title: A news article saying the average is 500만 원
y-m-73-03.goal: Realize that the mean alone cannot be used to judge the statement 'at least half earn more than a certain amount', say what additional information is needed, and make your own data that have the same mean but different conclusions.
y-m-73-03.material: There are 5 households in a village. One news article says 'The mean monthly income of households in this village (before tax, unit: 만 원) is 500', and the last sentence of the same article says 'At least half of the households in this village earn more than 400만 원 a month.' The income of each household is not given in the article. The monthly income of every household is at least 100만 원, and incomes are integers (in units of 만 원).
y-m-73-03.thinking.1: Making a counterexample with the same mean but a different distribution
y-m-73-03.thinking.2: Saying what additional information is needed
y-m-73-03.prereq.0: How to find the mean and the median (middle value)
y-m-73-03.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.prompt: Besides the mean of 500, what would you need to know to judge most directly whether the last sentence of the article is true?
y-m-73-03.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine two or three sets of 5 numbers that have the same mean but different shapes.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which of the 5 households, lined up in order of size, the words 'at least half' relate to.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.o.a: A value that double-checks how many households actually live in this village
y-m-73-03.s.s1.r.a: The number of households is already given as 5, and even with this value, the distribution cannot be seen from the mean.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.o.b: The monthly income of the household with the highest income
y-m-73-03.s.s1.r.b: The largest value tells you what pushes the mean up, but it does not tell you how the incomes of the other households are spread out.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.o.c: The monthly income of the household in the middle when incomes are lined up in order of size
y-m-73-03.s.s1.r.c: Whether at least half exceed a certain value is directly connected to the middle value when lined up in order of size. You found a representative value other than the mean.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.o.d: The mean of 500 calculated to two decimal places
y-m-73-03.s.s1.r.d: Even if you write the mean more precisely, you still cannot tell apart different distributions that have the same mean.
y-m-73-03.s.s1.explain: When 5 households are lined up in order of size, the 3rd household is in the middle. 'At least half earn more than 400' is the same as saying the income of the middle household is more than 400. The mean can be pulled strongly by one or two very high households, so it is not sufficient for this judgment. (Of course, knowing the income of every household would also be sufficient, but if you choose just one thing, it is the middle value.)
y-m-73-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different sets of 5 households whose mean is exactly 500 but for which the last sentence of the article ('at least half earn more than 400') is false. Enter the incomes in order from smallest as a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e. (The same value may appear more than once.)
y-m-73-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write five numbers so that the sum is 2500, and check what the middle number is when they are lined up in order of size.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.hint.1: Try out how the sum of the other four numbers changes if you make the largest number e large.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.var.a: Household with the least income (만 원)
y-m-73-03.s.s2.var.e: Household with the most income (만 원)
y-m-73-03.s.s2.ok.c1: They are in order from smallest, and all are integers of at least 100.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Write them in order from smallest (a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e), and all must be integers of at least 100.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the five numbers must be 2500 for the mean to be 500.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Fewer than half earn more than 400.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.fail.c3: If the middle household (c) is above 400, then 3 or more households are above 400. Look at what you should do with c for the article's statement to be false.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.explain: Example: (100, 200, 300, 400, 1500) has a sum of 2500 and a middle value of 300, so only 1 household earns more than 400. (400, 400, 400, 400, 900) has 4 households at '400 or less'. Since it says 'more than', a household at 400 is not one that earns more. Even with the same mean, if one household is very large, the others can be small.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Using the examples you made, write whether the information that the mean is 500 alone is enough to judge the last sentence of the article, and give your reason.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: For the example you made, write the mean, the middle household, and the largest household, one line each.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Also think of one set of 5 households with the same mean for which the article's sentence is true, and compare the two examples.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your explanation that in the example you made, the mean is 500 but the article's statement is false?
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you name the thing that is the reason, such as the 'middle household' or a 'very large value'?
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the fact that the article's sentence could be true (when the middle value is greater than 400)?
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.model.0: Even if the mean is 500, if one household is very high, such as 1500, the others can be low. In the example above, the mean is 500 but the middle household is 300. So the mean alone cannot tell whether half earn more than 400.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If the income of some households is very large, the mean is pulled up. The mean is 500, but 4 of the 5 households could be at 400 or less. Judging by the mean alone is not enough; you also have to look at the middle value.
y-m-73-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Does not mention the case where it is true, but meets the key point

y-m-73-04.title: A news article saying a raise in pay is a loss
y-m-73-04.topic: Tax rates by bracket (tax by income)
y-m-73-04.goal: Judge that whether take-home pay can fall after crossing into a bracket with a higher tax rate depends on which part the rate is applied to, and find the error in a solution that compared the two methods.
y-m-73-04.material: The monthly income tax rule of an imaginary country is as follows. If the monthly income is 1,000만 원 or less, the tax rate is 10%, and if it is over 1,000만 원, the tax rate is 20%. One news article reported that 'if monthly pay rises from 1,000만 원 to 1,100만 원, the tax becomes 220만 원 and take-home pay actually falls to 880만 원.' (Take-home pay = income − tax. The article does not say whether the 20% is multiplied by the 'whole income' or only by the 'part over 1,000만 원'. This rule is imaginary, made up for explanation, and is not the actual tax law.)
y-m-73-04.thinking.0: Finding the conditions under which the article's claim holds
y-m-73-04.prereq.1: The definition take-home pay = income − tax
y-m-73-04.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most fitting statement evaluating the content of the article.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put into words what the article's calculation (20% of the income) assumes the 20% is applied to.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the tax for 1,100만 원 in another way once more and compare the take-home pay.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.o.a: Income went up, so take-home pay must go up too, which means the article's calculation is wrong under any rule.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.r.a: You decided in advance that take-home pay rises when income rises. You did not test the cases in which that is not so, depending on how the tax is applied.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.o.b: If the 20% is multiplied by the whole income, it works out as the article says, but if it is multiplied only by the part over, it is different.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.r.b: You found the condition that the article's conclusion depends on how the tax is applied.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.o.c: The rate went up from 10% to 20%, so take-home pay falls no matter how the tax is applied.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.r.c: You linked the rise in the rate directly to the fall in take-home pay. You did not examine which part the higher rate is applied to.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.o.d: At 1,100만 원, the tax should be 10% of that amount, 110만 원, so the article's calculation is wrong.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.r.d: 1,100만 원 is over 1,000만 원, so it is in the bracket where 20% applies. The issue is the assumption, not the calculation itself.
y-m-73-04.s.s1.explain: 20% of 1,100 is 220, so the article's calculation is correct under the assumption that 'the 20% is multiplied by the whole income'. But if it is multiplied only by the part over, the tax is 1,000×10% + 100×20% = 120, so take-home pay actually goes up. If you do not know exactly which way the rule works, you cannot judge the article.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.prompt: A student compared the two methods. Choose one line that is wrong. (Method A: the 20% is multiplied by the whole income; Method B: it is multiplied only by the part over 1,000만 원)
y-m-73-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each line, recalculate income − tax to check that the income, tax, and take-home pay match.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the numbers to see in which method the take-home pay falls compared with 900.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.line.0: With an income of 1,000만 원 the rate is 10%, so the tax is 100만 원 and the take-home pay is 900만 원.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.line.1: Method A: 20% of an income of 1,100만 원 is 220만 원, so the take-home pay is 880만 원.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.line.2: Method B: up to 1,000만 원 it is 10%, so 100만 원, and for the 100만 원 over it is 20%, so 20만 원, which makes the tax 120만 원.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.line.3: Method B: the take-home pay is 1,100 − 120 = 990만 원.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.line.4: Therefore the method in which take-home pay can fall even though income rose is B.
y-m-73-04.s.s2.explain: Line 4 says 1,100 − 120 = 990, but it is 980, so the calculation is wrong. Line 5 is wrong because, looking at line 1 and line 2, the method in which take-home pay falls from 900 to 880 is A, but it says B. (In B it is 980, so it actually goes up.)

y-m-73-05.title: Can people's choices differ even when the expected values are the same?
y-m-73-05.goal: Explain that even when expected values are the same, choices can differ depending on how people feel about the risk of a large loss, and make your own conditions under which buying the insurance is a very slight gain in expected value.
y-m-73-05.material: If you use a phone for a year, its screen may break. As an imaginary case, the probability of breaking in one year is 6% (assume it can break at most once a year), and if it breaks, the repair cost is 40만 원. Damage insurance covers the full repair cost if you pay an annual premium of 2만 4천 원 (a deductible of 0원). Assume the probability is known exactly.
y-m-73-05.thinking.0: Calculating the expected value and interpreting its meaning
y-m-73-05.thinking.2: Judging by a standard other than expected value
y-m-73-05.prereq.0: Probability and expected value (sum of probability × value)
y-m-73-05.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.prompt: When you compare buying the insurance and not buying it by the 'expected value of the money spent in a year', what is the most fitting evaluation?
y-m-73-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write down all the possible spending amounts for a year without the insurance, and write the probability of each next to it.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.hint.1: Find the average of those cases and compare it with the premium, and think about what spending would actually come out if you look at just one year.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.o.a: The expected values are the same, so whichever you choose, the money you actually spend each year is exactly the same.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.r.a: The expected value is an average over many times. You missed that the actual spending in any one year can split into 0원 or 40만 원.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.o.b: 6% is a small probability, so the damage will not happen, and buying the insurance is just a loss.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.r.b: You turned a small probability into 'it will not happen'. The point of the problem is that even at 6%, if it happens it costs a large amount.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.o.c: The premium is much smaller than the repair cost, so buying the insurance is unconditionally a gain.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.r.c: You compared only the sizes of the premium and the repair cost. You must multiply by the probability that repair is needed to make an average comparison.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.o.d: The expected values are the same so neither is better, and what separates the choices is whether you want to avoid the risk of a large cost.
y-m-73-05.s.s1.r.d: You found the standard that remains when the expected values are the same (how much risk you can bear).
y-m-73-05.s.s1.explain: Without the insurance, the expected repair cost is 0.06 × 40만 = 2만 4천 원, the same as the premium. On average neither is better, but without the insurance there is a 6% chance that 40만 원 comes out all at once. How much someone wants to avoid this risk depends on the person and the situation.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.prompt: Let the probability of damage be p% and the repair cost be r 만 원. The premium stays at 2만 4천 원, and enter 3 different pairs (p, r) for which the expected repair cost without the insurance (= r × p/100, in 만 원) is greater than the premium but at most 3만 원 (the gain is very small). p is an integer from 1 to 50, and r is an integer from 10 to 100.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one probability p and one repair cost r, calculate p × r, and compare it with 240 and 300.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.hint.1: If you have found one pair that satisfies the condition, change p and adjust r to find another pair.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.ok.c1: p and r are integers within the range.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be an integer from 1 to 50, and r must be an integer from 10 to 100.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The expected repair cost is greater than the premium of 2.4만 원.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The expected repair cost (r × p/100) must be greater than 2.4만 원. Check whether p × r is greater than 240.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The expected repair cost is at most 3만 원.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The expected repair cost is over 3만 원. Reduce one of them so that p × r is at most 300.
y-m-73-05.s.s2.explain: The expected repair cost r × p/100 must be more than 2.4 and at most 3, so p × r must be more than 240 and at most 300. Examples: (7, 40) gives 2.8만 원, (10, 30) gives 3만 원, (6, 50) gives 3만 원, and (5, 60) also gives 3만 원. (6, 40) gives 2.4만 원, which is the same as the premium, so it is not 'greater'.
y-m-73-05.s.s3.prompt: In the situation of s1 (the expected values are the same), choose either 'buy the insurance' or 'do not buy the insurance', assume the situation of a person for whom doing so is reasonable, and write the reason along with numbers.
y-m-73-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the spending in a year when it breaks without the insurance and in a year when it does not break.
y-m-73-05.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine how you would feel if that 40만 원 took up a large share of your bank account.
y-m-73-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If a student whose monthly allowance is ... then ...
y-m-73-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you accept that the expected values are the same and name a standard other than that?
y-m-73-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do the circumstances you assumed and the choice connect with each other?
y-m-73-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you consider that a person who makes the opposite choice can also be reasonable?
y-m-73-05.s.s3.model.0: For a student whose allowance is 10만 원 a month, it is hard to bear a sudden cost of 40만 원. Even though the average is the same, 2만 4천 원 removes the risk of a large expense, so buying the insurance is reasonable.
y-m-73-05.s.s3.model.1: A person with 200만 원 in savings can get through even if 40만 원 goes out. When the probability is 6%, the average cost is the same as the premium, so there is no need to pay it, and over the long run the money spent becomes similar, so it is fine not to buy the insurance.

y-m-73-06.title: Should the person who is better at everything take on all the work?
y-m-73-06.topic: Opportunity cost and division of labor
y-m-73-06.goal: When both people can work only the same number of hours, find several ways to divide the time that reach the target output, and explain with opportunity cost why each person's work is divided up.
y-m-73-06.material: There are two people, A and B, who make cookies and cakes. Each works exactly 8 hours (an integer number of hours) a day, and in one hour they make only cookies or only cakes. The output per hour is 12 cookies or 4 cakes for A, and 6 cookies or 3 cakes for B. The daily target is at least 72 cookies and at least 29 cakes in total for the two of them. If both spend 4 hours on cookies and 4 hours on cakes, they make 72 cookies and 28 cakes, which is 1 cake short.
y-m-73-06.thinking.1: Finding the rule the solutions have in common
y-m-73-06.prereq.0: Linear expression calculation (hours × output per hour)
y-m-73-06.prereq.1: Testing two inequalities at the same time
y-m-73-06.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different time allocations that reach the target. a is the number of hours A spends making cookies, and b is the number of hours B spends making cookies (the remaining hours are for cakes). a and b are integers from 0 to 8.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.hint.0: First pick an a, and then try out how small b must be at most to make at least 29 cakes.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each solution you find, write the number of cookies and cakes in a table and check that both targets are met.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 8.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 0 to 8.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.fail.c2: There are fewer than 72 cookies. Find the number of cookies by multiplying A's and B's cookie hours by the output per hour and adding them.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.fail.c3: There are fewer than 29 cakes. The cake hours are 8 minus the cookie hours.
y-m-73-06.s.s1.explain: The only (a, b) that satisfy the conditions are the three pairs (5, 2), (6, 0), and (6, 1). For example: (5, 2) gives 60+12=72 cookies and 12+18=30 cakes. (7, 0) gives 84 cookies but 28 cakes, which is 1 short. In all of them, A spends more time on cookies and B spends more time on cakes.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.prompt: In the solutions you found, A spent more time on cookies and B spent more time on cakes. A is better than B at making both, so what is the most fitting reason it is good for B to take on the cakes?
y-m-73-06.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate how many cookies A can make in the time A takes to make one cake, and how many B can, and compare them.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.hint.1: In the solutions you found, try out how many cookies and cakes would change if you swapped A's and B's cake hours.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.o.a: For each cake, A gives up 3 cookies and B gives up 2, so it is better for B to take it on.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.r.a: You compared, for each person, how much of one thing they give up by making the other. This is the idea of dividing up by the amount given up rather than by who is better.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.o.b: B makes 6 cookies, more than 3 cakes per hour, so B should focus on cookies.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.r.b: You looked only at the fact that B alone makes more cookies than cakes. A also makes more cookies (12) than cakes (4), so this reason alone does not decide who takes on what.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.o.c: A is better at both, so B should rest and A should make both.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.r.c: You missed the condition that A's available time per day is fixed at 8 hours. It is hard for A alone to meet the target.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.o.d: If B takes on the cakes, B works fewer hours, so total output actually increases.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.r.d: B's working time is always the same 8 hours. The explanation that output increases because the time decreases does not match the conditions.
y-m-73-06.s.s2.explain: A gives up 3 cookies (12 ÷ 4) for 1 cake, and B gives up 2 cookies (6 ÷ 3). If B makes the cakes, fewer cookies are given up to make the same cakes, so total output increases. Conversely, for cookies, A gives up fewer cakes than B. The standard is not how good someone is but 'the amount of the other thing given up'.

y-m-73-07.title: Does 'inflation slows for the third year in a row' mean prices got cheaper?
y-m-73-07.goal: Tell apart the level of prices from the speed at which prices rise, and, using the numbers in the table, correct a news headline in a way a middle-school student can understand.
y-m-73-07.material:
The headline of one news article is 'Inflation slows for the third year in a row'. The consumer price index (with 2021 as 100; imaginary data) is as follows. Read the table in the order year, price index, rate of increase from the previous year. The rate of increase is rounded to one decimal place.

Year | Price index (2021=100) | Rate of increase from previous year
2021 | 100.0 | -
2022 | 105.0 | 5.0%
2023 | 108.5 | 3.3%
2024 | 110.6 | 1.9%

(Rate of increase from the previous year = by what % that year's index is greater than the previous year's index. Assume the cost of buying the same goods is proportional to the price index.)
y-m-73-07.thinking.0: Telling apart level and rate of change
y-m-73-07.thinking.1: Separating what the table can say from what it cannot
y-m-73-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a percent rate of change
y-m-73-07.prereq.2: The H3 label on this task is only a difficulty marker for this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. Assumption: a student meeting economics math at a high-school level for the first time.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that can be said for certain from the table alone.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read only the price index column from top to bottom, and check whether the numbers got bigger or smaller.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.hint.1: Read the rate-of-increase column separately, and tell whether each statement is about the index or about the rate of increase.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.o.a: The price level in 2024 became lower than in 2022.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.r.a: The price index rose from 105.0 to 110.6. You read the rate of increase getting smaller as meaning the same thing as the price level going down.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.o.b: The price level in 2024 is higher than in 2023.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.r.b: You read the fact that the index rose from 108.5 to 110.6. You understood that when the rate of increase is positive (+), the level goes up.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.o.c: The rate of increase has kept getting smaller, so prices will fall in 2025.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.r.c: You took the trend of the past three years as a sure result for next year. The table has no information about 2025.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.o.d: The amount (in percent) by which prices rose each year gradually got smaller.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.r.d: You read the change in the rates of increase 5.0%, 3.3%, 1.9%. This is a statement about the size of the rise, not about the level.
y-m-73-07.s.s1.explain: From 2022 to 2024 the price index kept rising: 105.0 → 108.5 → 110.6 (b). The rate of increase got smaller: 5.0%, 3.3%, 1.9% (d). But a smaller rate of increase does not mean the price level went down (a is false). The table cannot tell what will happen in 2025 (c).
y-m-73-07.s.s2.prompt: A friend saw the article and said, 'Prices keep going down, so groceries will get cheaper now.' In 2 to 3 sentences, write an explanation that corrects the meaning of the headline, using one or two numbers from the table, so that even a younger middle-school sibling can understand.
y-m-73-07.s.s2.hint.0: First write one sentence comparing the price indexes of 2022 and 2024.
y-m-73-07.s.s2.hint.1: Rewrite 'the rate of increase got smaller' with an everyday comparison, such as 'the speed got slower'.
y-m-73-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Prices did not go down, but ...
y-m-73-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart the 'price (price level)' and the 'speed of rising'?
y-m-73-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the numbers you took from the table are right?
y-m-73-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write in words a middle-school student can read (did you add explanations to difficult words)?
y-m-73-07.s.s2.model.0: Prices did not go down; they kept going up. From 105.0 in 2022 to 110.6 in 2024, so things got more expensive. It is just that the amount of the rise each year got smaller: 5.0%, 3.3%, 1.9%.
y-m-73-07.s.s2.model.1: The article means that the speed at which prices rise has slowed. 2023 is 108.5 and 2024 is 110.6, so the price itself still went up. It did not get cheaper.
y-m-73-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: An explanation put in terms of 'speed'
